challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: Approval and escalation are treated as new functionality to build on leave requests.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has an absence module and approval circuits shared across modules. If a circuit exists, even one not switched on, the work may be configuring it and adding an escalation rule rather than building an approval step. Checking this first could shrink or reshape the whole build.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel approval path duplicates shared logic and creates two sources of truth that diverge, and a change to the shared circuit may break other modules.
challenges.recommendation: Review the current absence module and approval circuit configuration with the client before estimating anything.

challenges.headline: Approval as a single click
challenges.premise: A manager's approval is a simple yes/no on the request.
challenges.alternative: For leave on this platform, approval is likely to involve a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) and possibly several approval levels by leave type or duration. Deciding up front whether the first release is only the yes/no with escalation, or includes the balance check, keeps the scope honest.
challenges.consequence: If the balance check and multi-level rules are assumed absent and then required, the build changes shape late. If they are assumed present and are not, the first release carries cost nobody asked for.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client whether balance validation and leave-type rules are in scope, and fix the first release accordingly.

challenges.headline: What 'away' means
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away, without saying how.
challenges.alternative: Three readings lead to different builds. Reading it from the manager's own approved leave is deterministic. A self-set out-of-office flag depends on managers remembering to set it. No response after N days works as a timer and needs no availability data at all. A timer fallback can also cover the other two readings.
challenges.consequence: Escalating only on the manager's own leave misses a manager who is simply unresponsive. A timer alone makes a request wait N days even when the manager is known to be on holiday.
challenges.recommendation: Agree the trigger with the client before design. One option to put to them is a timer that fires immediately if the manager is on approved leave.

Leave decisions touch French labour rules on paid leave and RTT, and HR data under GDPR, so visibility of requests to the backup approver needs care.

challenges.premise: Escalation is a new feature to build for leave requests.
challenges.alternative: The approval circuits are already shared across modules and client-specific. Delegation, a fallback approver or a timeout may already exist but be switched off for absences. Checking this first could turn a build into a configuration.
challenges.consequence: A parallel escalation mechanism built inside the absence module would duplicate the circuit logic and diverge from the other modules that share it.
challenges.recommendation: Review what the current circuit supports for absences and for delegation before estimating anything.

challenges.headline: Undefined meaning of 'away'
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away and escalate accordingly.
challenges.alternative: Two simpler triggers are available: a manager-set delegate while on leave, or a timeout with no response. Each is a distinct build. Detecting absence automatically from the manager's own approved leave is a third option, but it makes approval depend on another leave record being up to date.
challenges.consequence: If 'away' is left open, the team may build a time-driven engine when a delegate field would do, or the reverse, and requests still get stuck when the declaration is forgotten.
challenges.recommendation: Agree with the client on one primary trigger, and treat the others as fallbacks only if needed.

challenges.headline: Approval without a balance check
challenges.premise: Approval is a manager's yes or no on the request.
challenges.alternative: Treat the decision as manager approval plus a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) at the point the decision is made, with the escalation approver bound by the same check.
challenges.consequence: Without it, an escalated approver can approve leave the employee has no balance for, and it is only caught later by HR.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm where the balance check sits relative to the escalation step before designing states.

challenges.headline: Building before checking existing circuits
challenges.premise: Manager approval with escalation is treated as a new feature to build.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has absence management and shared approval circuits. Configuring the existing circuit, or adding one escalation step to it, may deliver most of this at a fraction of the effort. This is my reasoning from the product context, and the client has not said whether the circuit was considered.
challenges.consequence: A parallel approval flow would duplicate the shared circuit, create inconsistent behavior across modules, and add permission rules that must be maintained twice.
challenges.recommendation: Audit what the current approval circuit already does for leave, and list only the gap, before estimating any build.

challenges.headline: Undefined meaning of 'away'
challenges.premise: 'If the manager is away' is taken as a clear, detectable condition.
challenges.alternative: Three readings are possible: the manager is on approved leave, the manager has set a delegate, or the manager has not answered after N days. Escalating on a time delay alone is simpler and needs no availability data. Escalating on leave status depends on the manager's own absence records. This document has not chosen between them; the client must.
challenges.consequence: The leave-status reading couples the manager's own requests to everyone else's, and it fails when the manager is away but has no recorded leave. The delay reading can escalate when the manager is merely busy.
challenges.recommendation: Decide the trigger with the client first. A delay-based trigger with an optional delegate is a lower-risk starting proposal.

challenges.headline: Approval as a single decision
challenges.premise: Approval is assumed to be only the manager's yes or no.
challenges.alternative: On this platform, approval usually brings a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) and possibly more than one level. Confirming whether the manager's decision is the only check settles scope early.
challenges.consequence: A balance check discovered late changes the data model, adds concurrency on balance updates, and raises French labor-law exposure.
challenges.recommendation: Ask whether balance checks and leave-type rules are in scope, or deliberately deferred to the existing absence logic.

Per-client variation in approval and escalation rules could turn a small change into a configurable engine.
An undefined trigger and target lead to rework late in the build.

opportunities.text: Make escalation a reusable capability of the shared approval circuit (trigger, target, timing) rather than a leave-specific feature.
Reuse the client and contact role model for notification routing to escalation approvers.

next_steps: Audit how leave approval works today and what the existing approval circuit already covers, to size the real gap.
Settle with the client what 'away' means, who the escalation target is and after what delay.
Confirm whether balance and quota checks, and per-client configuration, are in scope for this release.
Define the loop and double-decision edge cases and write acceptance scenarios for them before build.

decisions.decision: Managers approve or reject their employees' leave requests, identified through the reporting line.
Extend the existing absence module and shared approval circuit rather than build a separate approval flow.
decisions.why: The platform already has both, and a parallel flow would duplicate shared permission and approval rules.
decisions.tradeoff: Dependence on the shared circuit's limits and the risk of affecting other modules, in exchange for consistency and less build.
